div.head: Authors
div.p: Dr Cécile Chevalier, Dr Irene Fubara-Manuel, and Dr Sharon Webb (University of Sussex)

div.head: Abstract
div.p: The scaling-up, speeding-up, and powering-up of technology, that are all coterminous to the hegemonic cycle of infrastructural development, makes the prospect of building differently, (im)possible. In this paper, we explore whether autonomous feminist infrastructures can exist in the current technological milieu, which is dominated by large tech companies whose values and approaches are only determined by profit and the bottom line. We ask what negotiations with existing infrastructures does feminist technological autonomy require? What further constraints emerge in creating these autonomous infrastructures that confront and challenge the hegemonic systems of technology? We locate a 'feminist autonomous system' as one that resonates with Wilson’s (2016) conceptualisation of intimacy, infrastructure, and power. Feminist autonomous systems acknowledge the relational role of infrastructure, in bridging and walling out communities. We focus specifically on feminist servers as a case study which draws from our work on Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities (DH). As a relational system, servers encourage agency around access, preservation and management of data. Our paper is a situated critical reflection based on our experimentation. It expands on our successes and failures of building autonomous feminist servers as a means of emphasising the need for a plurality of infrastructures and an exploration of the socio-technical entanglements in which such infrastructures exist.

div.head: Pretext
div.p: When we choose not to invest in our own infrastructure, we choose not to articulate a different possible version of the world (Posner, 2016)

Building autonomous feminist infrastructures, such as autonomous feminist servers, is a way to foster agency from technological gatekeepers, it is a means to redistribute power, and build shared sustainable heritage. Critically, it is also a way to queer and reorient technological optimisation, recognizing the ongoing need for more equitable technological environments. Such equitable environments ensure that women, including trans-women and fem identified individuals, can have agency in current and future techno-societal contributions and imaginaries. As such, this paper explores our experiments with autonomous feminist servers. Authorship is listed in alphabetic order – authors contributed equally to developing, writing, and editing this paper, contributing equally their expertise. In addition, we acknowledge the work and contributions of Ranju Upadhyay, FSF Programmer (Maynooth University) and Alex Peverett, FSF Research Technician (University of Sussex) - their contributions to developing the FSF-Server have been invaluable. It builds on prior and ongoing foundational work/heritage, including work from TransHackFeminist, Syster Server, Winnie Soon, Mara Karagianni, Sophie Toupin, MariaLab, among others. The work described here, therefore, represents a single component of a larger ecosystem investigating autonomous feminist infrastructures - success in these (im)possibilities depends on collective action, ethics of care, knowledge sharing and forms of decentring and/or decentralisation, as social change. The work challenges the current logic of technological optimisation that continues to raise gendered, intersectional, and multiple layers of oppressions and omissions. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun (Chun and Cotte, 2020), for instance, critiques this logic of optimisation in machine learning through unpacking the claim that ‘“based on the past, we can predict the future”’. Chun notes that ML does not predict but instead “automate[s] the future” using biased data from the past which is accumulated and optimised into algorithmic truth. Social and technical injustice is not resolved, instead, they are applied at fast speed and at scale to become efficient in discrimination. Within this context, the desire of building digital infrastructures outside of the logics of optimisation and capitalist accumulation arises.

Framing, imagining, and building our own digital infrastructures, we break down this paper into four sections that expand on: our situated knowledge and histories; the power of affect in building feminist infrastructures (servers specifically); our orientations and negotiations of autonomy; and how we build our own feminist infrastructure together. The first section frames the context in which we imagined our autonomous feminist server as a part of Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities FSFDH is a project funded by the UK research council, AHRC, and the Irish Research council, IRC under their ‘UK-Ireland Collaboration in the Digital Humanities Research Grants Call’ (grant numbers AH/W001667/1 and IRC/W001667/1). In the second section, we address the role of affect in building feminist infrastructures. We establish our thinking acknowledging that infrastructure organises social life. We unpack infrastructural failures from Black feminist perspectives that note the embeddedness of racially discriminatory glitches in contemporary technologies. Failure, here, is not an exception to infrastructure, but actually a discursive tool to naturalise existing infrastructures and close off alternate infrastructures — making them seem impossible. Expanding on feminist servers as a prime example of feminist infrastructures, we point to a constellation of transformative practices that demonstrate other possibilities of connectivity, autonomy, and optimisation. Following from this discussion, the third section focuses on the (im)possibility of ‘autonomy’. It (re)orients technological optimisation, towards a focus that prioritises the humanities over the digital – that is critical digital humanities. With this in mind, we draw from Ahmed’s (2006) queer phenomenology as a framework to contextualise and rationalise autonomous feminist servers and situated knowledge and lived experiences from the borders. As a framework it ‘reorients’ aspects of technological care to model and foster social change, which make possible techno feminist heritage and legacies. Finally, in the fourth section, we return to the work carried out by the Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities team. In this section we explore some of the practical considerations and the approaches we took to building and (re)claiming hardware/software ‘down to the code’ (vale, 2020, p. 75). As we critically reflect on our experiments, we explore the (im)possibilities of hosting the project’s archive (created in Omeka) on our own, purpose built, autonomous feminist server. We contemplate the importance of divesting, decentring, and disentangling our heritage, remembering that ‘memory and archiving is empowering’, as noted in the TransHackFeminist (THF!) Convergence Report (2015). In essence, we wanted to inhabit the process of making, of building together, where we could learn with, from, and for each other. Through the process of speculative building, we wanted to consider the sustainability and the potential losses and gains of such a move. We recognised that being critical is a privilege, acknowledging that sometimes there is no viable alternative.

div.head: Troubled Histories: Technology and Gender Bias
div.p: Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities (FSF) is a collaborative project, inspired by a history of intersectional feminist interventions in technology. It places significant importance on forms of critical digital humanities and is one of three (out of a total of 11) projects within the AHRC-IRC collaborative call which frame a feminist intervention in DH as critical and timely Other feminist-oriented projects in this call include, Women in Focus (https://www.uea.ac.uk/groups-and-centres/projects/women-in-focus/about-us) and Feminist Art Making Histories (https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=AH%2FW001810%2F1). This context is significant in terms of the broader landscape in current DH praxis and method - that is, DH, as a discipline, is coming to terms with its histories and embracing the need to engage with queer, feminist, and de-colonial praxis. These interventions are threaded in the work of several DH scholars, including Jacqueline Wernimont (2013), Roopika Risam (2015), Tara McPherson (2017), Elizabeth Losh and Jacqueline Wernimont (2019), Caroline Bassett, Sarah Kember, and Kate O’Riordan (2019), Barbara Bordalejo and Roopika Risam (2019), Dorothy Kim and Adeline Koh (2021), among others. Their publications, and the various queer, feminist and de-colonial theories they draw from and develop, reflect a significant shift in the socio-cultural politics of DH – that is who is doing it, for what purposes, and in terms of who, fundamentally, benefits. This landscape of critical digital humanities is, however, reflective of the broader state of computational technology which is entrenched with bias, generated unconsciously or otherwise, and whose current trajectory requires remapping.

We view ‘Full Stack Feminism’ as a means to encourage a critique of the ‘tools, systems, and codes we (re)use’, and ‘the patriarchal, ultra-capitalist, neo-liberal, heteronormative social, cultural and political eco-systems' in which we/they exist (Webb, 2023b). It is a reminder of the need to ‘critique all layers of our social, cultural and technological infrastructures’, and calls for a commitment to review and critique all stages of the development and data life cycle and to (re)consider elements of practice across these areas from an intersectional feminist perspective (Webb, 2023b). In doing so, it contributes to the ever-expanding field of intersectional feminist, and queer, digital humanities.

Beyond the parameters of DH, FSF stems from the experience of team members working across disciplinary boundaries - history and computer science, digital media and creative practice, critical theory and coding - and their experiences of work with technology and as technologists, in various environments. Our histories as a team, and the histories which have erased women’s contributions to the development of computational technologies, are a significant motivating factor for FSF and for the development of autonomous feminist infrastructures, as explored in this paper. The sheer abundance of literature on this subject underscores the enormity of the issue and the daunting task required to address it, naming Judy Wajcman (2004), Cathy O’Neill (2016), Mar Hicks (2017), Taina Bucher (2018), Safiya Umoja Noble (2018), Ruja Benjamin (2019), Jennifer L. Eberhardt (2019), Hannah Fry (2019), Wendy Hui Kyong Chun (2021), among others. Much of this work is influenced, and stems from intersectional feminist thinking and praxis, critical race and decolonial theory, as well as social justice and equity work. In line with FSF, this work recognises how current computational systems are entangled with our socio-cultural and socio-political pasts. Through forms of digitisation, whether digitisation of canonical western texts for machine learning, or the digitisation of our thoughts in software code and software logics, we have transferred and embedded the ingrained biases of society into bias in our digital spaces. This raises questions of who can inhabit future technological imaginaries – as raised by Chun earlier in our text, and also questions of whose heritage and legacy becomes prioritised. The wider socio-technical context of computing shows this history of power imbalances.

The processes of digitisation, through coding and recoding, often replicate traditional power structures, instead of radically overhauling them (O’Neil, 2016; Chun, 2021). These result in, on the surface, relatively benign and unassuming software systems which discriminate as a result of statistical anomalies and assumptions. Such anomalies, however, cause significant harm to certain communities of identity. Specifically, we can look to surveillance technologies (Eberhardt, 2019), insurance and banking systems (O’Neil, 2016), as well as judicial decision-making algorithms (Benjamin, 2019) which cause significant harm to African American communities. Racists stereotyping because of algorithmic sorting and ranking, or racist profiling because of bias, skewed, and decontextualised data, is but one part of the technological kaleidoscope of biased stereotyping, and profiling. Benjamin, in Race After Technology (2019), notes that discriminatory practices precede software and hardware design, and are rooted in historical legal and social codes. Algorithmic bias mirrors society’s entrenched biases, reflecting historic discrimination.
Technology is wedded to ideology. When people create something, they are imposing their orientation on the world through their invention (Alkalimat, 2021, p. 7).

This imposition of specific world orientations often stems from biased user profiling, which designs technology to cater to a default user (often cis-male, heterosexual, white, middle-class), resulting in systems that work for some and often exclude minoritised others. Such biased profiling can be traced back to traditional phenomenology, which perceives our experiences of the world as a norm, neutral and objective. Ahmed’s (2006) conceptualisation of queer phenomenology, however, underscores the absurdity of asserting that our individual and collective experiences are anything but biased and skewed, and calls for us to include different perspectives. For example, the Strava fitness app, was designed with biases favouring male, cisgender, straight, white, and abled individuals (Spinks, 2017)). It inadvertently endangered women’s safety by default-sharing personal details with nearby users. In the FSF ‘Feminist Coding and Making’ Workshops (2023-24, held on-line over five sessions), the team research associate and freelance developer Suze Shardlow, expanded on the Strava example (Shardlow and Webb, 2024). In the coding workshops we invited participants to scrutinise the software development life cycle through a feminist lens. We discussed how a feminist-oriented Software Developer Life Cycle (SDLC) could have identified and addressed such biases more effectively. In essence, we deduced that who develops the software intrinsically affects the implicit biases of the technology.

As feminist computer historians such as Mar Hicks (2017) have documented, computing is a male dominated profession. Their research, alongside that of Claire L. Evans (2018) and others, trace the historical factors behind the ongoing gender gap in computer science and software engineering fields (Webb, 2023a). The feminisation (meaning devaluation) and masculinisation of certain labour because of past bureaucratic and fiscal decisions (Hicks, 2017), coupled with the erasure of women in computing histories (Evans, 2018; Kleiman, 2022) and the marketisation of computers as a male orientated pursuit during the 1970s and 80s, as well as other aggravating factors, mean that as of 2023, only 19% of computing degree applicants in UK higher education were female (Women into Science and Engineering, 2023). This demographic unevenness (in the UK, Europe and US at least), is of course part of a longer historical narrative which perpetuates and relies on the myth that women are not technologists or software developers (Jane and Fisher, 2003; Aspray, 2016; Abbate, 2017), despite their significant contributions to the development of early computing (Edwards and Harris, 2016; Hicks, 2017; Kleiman, 2022). While an extensive history of women’s erasure from computing is out of scope for this paper, it is a significant motivating factor of the research reframed here, and that of FSF more broadly. Noting this history, both from the perspective of women’s contributions and their subsequent exclusion from computing histories, is crucial to understanding current technological problems, and informing their socio-technical solutions.

From the above cited scholarship, it is evident that our current digital ecosystems are a result of historic processes. These processes not only define our present but also predict our future (Chun and Cotte, 2020). The above histories show that technologies are not always reflective, representative of, or work for those traditionally, or continually, marginalised in our societies. The work of organisations such as the Algorithmic Justice League challenges the current maelstrom. The founder, Joy Buolamwini posits in an interview (Tucker, 2017), “we don’t have to bring the structural inequalities of the past into the future we create, but that’s only going to happen if we are intentional”. FSF supports this statement, and recognises that the socio-technical stacks of bias, oppression, and discrimination are historic. A way to reorient technology, however, is as The Feminist Principles of the Internet state–to understand the machine and to (re)claim it ‘down to the code’ (vale, 2020).

div.head: Full Stack Feminism
div.p: Reclaiming technologies ‘down to the code’ reflects the FSF-Framework, which is composed of three interconnecting, related but distinct stacks: (1) data and archives; (2) infrastructure, tools and code; and (3) access, experience, and integration. For more information on Full Stack Feminism, including a broader discussion of the stacks please see https://fullstackfeminismdh.pubpub.org/

Our stacks are not linear and do not progress necessarily in a sequence but provide a framework and focus for analysis and action - they are touchstones, references points, sites to prompt discussion and conversation. Each represents critical pressure points which we, as a research team, have identified through our experiences. The motivations and inspiration for Full Stack Feminism are multiple and varied, and are as much motivated by personal experiences - the personal is always political - as they are by high-level, “our digital technologies are riddled with problems and bias” warnings and alarms. This articulation represents our ‘feminist version of objectivity’ (Webb, 2023a).

The work described in this paper, therefore, is primarily focused on aspects of the stack of ‘infrastructure, tools, and code’ – since it considers the underlying architectures, systems and code upon which digital projects and systems rely on, and questions these from an intersectional feminist perspective. For example, questions and/or provocations which arise from infrastructure, tools, and code includes:

list.item: How mono-linguistic software languages affect how code is produced and re-used? What are the implications of the monopolisation of web infrastructures by western tech giants (e.g. Amazon AWS, Microsoft Azure) (Statista, 2024)?
What skills and understanding are lost by increased levels of abstraction which hide the complexities of software code in services such as web development serviced by ever evolving AI agents?

How can we disentangle, or indeed refuse, technological services which align themselves with or support the military industrial complex, war, and/or genocide (e.g. WIX’s #standwithisrael campaign which ignores the Palestinian plight and ongoing Israeli occupation of Palestinian land) (Wix, 2024), or indeed Google and Amazon selling cloud storage for abhorrent uses? (Anonymous Google and Amazon workers, 2021)
Additionally, how can we disentangle from, or refuse, technology that is built on extractive practices and labour conditions (such as the exploitation of indigenous women in the production of electronic devices) (Nakamura, 2014), as well as environmental injustices in computing (e.g. Large Language Models such as GPT2/3 that require high energy cost) (Bender et al, 2021)?

How do we refuse social media platforms, which provide visibility on the one hand but whose policies and algorithms also censor and make invisible certain content (e.g. Instagram, among other platforms, whose algorithms are known to shadow ban Queer, Trans, bodies, among others, as well as censoring queer content as pornographic whilst also banning sex positive content and breast-feeding images?) (Braidwood, 2018; Lee, 2020; Are, 2024).

div.p: Of course, these are just a fraction of the known political, social, and cultural bias which seep into the technologies we use on a daily basis - refusing these technologies is not always an option. As Toupin and Hache (2015, p. 22) states:

Using corporate services such as Facebook or Twitter may be very convenient, and at times strategic because they are generally provided for free and because this is where the so-called critical masses are. But using them also means accepting their terms of service, which are primarily shaped by profit, and in which human rights and gender social justice still remain of negligible importance. When using these online services, we and our networks are at their mercy, which means we cannot fully control our data, social networks and historical memories (or traces) on the internet.

It is from this position, influenced by our own questioning and that of others, we ask what are the (im)possibilities of autonomous feminist infrastructures? Can we exist outside of these technological dead-zones? Additionally,

[how] ...can we build and maintain autonomous feminist servers within (im)possible constraints? What negotiations with existing infrastructures does feminist technological autonomy require? What further constraints emerge in creating these autonomous servers? (Chevalier et al, 2023).

What do we lose when we remove ourselves from these sites of power, and what do we gain when we seek out and create our own alternatives, or in this instance, create feminist servers as an alternative to corporate ones. Specifically, we wanted to experiment with developing and utilising our own server space to host a project archive, and in so doing question the politics of power in both building and maintaining such a space. Grounded in our histories and influenced by our collective situated knowledge or contexts, the next section explores infrastructures, not just as a physical construction, but as the embodiment of the affective politics and desires of those which build them.

div.head: Feminist Infrastructures: The Affective Power of Servers
div.p: I’m very much interested in owning the domains, owning the understanding [of] how to upkeep the information that we’re building and making, and how to have the community hold those memories themselves rather than have to outsource to a national archive (Brathwaite-Shirley, 2023).

The impulse to understand the power relations behind building objects and the factors that result in their functioning, is evident in the field of Infrastructure Studies. ‘Infrastructure’ is not only a word that connects an interdisciplinary field of research, it also has meaning in quotidian contexts that is often a subject of satire in popular media. At the launch event of the Full Stack Feminism in Digital Humanities project, we adapted an XKCD comic frequently shared on computer programmer forums (see Figure 1). While the original comic pointed to ‘A project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003’ as the precariously thin block that held up the Jenga-like stack that made up modern digital infrastructure, our adaptation pointed to patriarchy, capitalism, colonial racism, and systemic injustice as the foundations of this stack. As our project both reappropriates the metaphor of the stack from web development and expands on the stack as a critical tool in analysis of technoculture (Terranova, 2014; Bratton, 2016; Liu, 2020; Webb, 2023a), this image served as an entry point and visual epistemology of the socio-technical stack of digital infrastructure. That noted, if infrastructure can be a punchline in geek comics, surely it is a subject with enough charge to power critical feminist analysis.
Figure 1: ‘Sociotechnical Dependencies’ Adapted from ‘Dependency’ by xkcd comic. (Creative Commons Licence: CC BY-NC 2.5)

Activated by this charge, our critical understanding of infrastructure sits within a genealogy that begins from the influential work of the ethnographer of infrastructure, Susan Leigh Star. Star’s (1999) article encourages a reading of infrastructure that does not simply study calcified roads, pipes, and cables, but also examines their role as part of everyday life. Infrastructural readings are common in contemporary feminist analysis of digital technology. For example, if comments are part of an infrastructure of technical documentation, the analysis of code in Easter (2018) examines how misogyny can be built into a programming language. On the other hand, projects such as Queering Bash (Soon and Karagianni, 2023) which subvert the Bourne Again Shell (Bash) language used in the highly technical field of Systems Administration, demonstrate how communities of queer creative coders can use the command line interface to express desire through code poetry. Such analysis and interventions of digital infrastructure illustrate that through relational readings, infrastructure becomes uncalcified from a ‘system of substrates’ to an active ‘part of human organisation’ (Star, 1999, p. 380).

As is the process with any developing field, early scholarship sees expansion and challenges to key concepts. In their influential article, Star (1999) outlines some of the characteristics of infrastructure, including the notion that infrastructure is a hidden substrate that becomes visible on breakdown. This conceptualisation of invisibility until failure, has been the focus of critique, as it assumes that failure is a unique event in functioning infrastructure. This understanding posits that infrastructures such as public trains fade into the background of everyday transportation until there is a problem on the line. Anyone who has experienced the everyday glitches of the British railway system–from trespassers on the tracks to industrial actions to signalling problems–might argue that failure is sometimes a defining part of infrastructure. Within such glitch-filled arrangements, infrastructure never truly fades into the background. Some broken systems were never broken. The prison abolition activist Miriam Kaba (2021) emphasises this in relation to the anti-Blackness in the US judicial infrastructure. Kaba notes that the rhetoric of brokenness places reform as the sensible choice in place of more transformative alternatives. In the same vein, Noble (2018) and Benjamin (2019) have expanded on glitches that harm Black women as a feature (and not a bug) of discriminatory technology in the larger structure of systemic racism.

Addressing the role of glitches and failures in infrastructure, we turn to cultural critic Lauren Berlant (2016). Berlant places their analysis of infrastructure in ‘troubling troubled times’ (2016, p. 395) where global social movements against racism, xenophobia, austerity, and capitalist exploitation point to an ‘infrastructural breakdown of modernist practices of resource distribution, social relation, and affective continuity’ (2016, p. 394). Berlant theorises that broken infrastructures reveal the opportunities for repair or abandonment for alternate options. In this sense, infrastructure does not simply sit still. For Berlant, infrastructure is always moving and transforming. The process of ‘infrastructure-making’ is a social and political action of ‘assemblage and use’ that transforms and organises the world (Berlant, 2016, p. 403). However, affect poses a tension as collective desire is mobilised for the repair and maintenance of some projects and ambivalence or disdain is mobilised for the failure of other infrastructures.

Similar to Berlant (2016), other feminist scholars have shown the importance of making the connection between failure, affect, and infrastructure. Ara Wilson (2016, p. 262) notes ‘infrastructure is repurposed toward intimacies we cherish and toward those we don’t.’ Public washrooms, in Wilson’s (2016) case study, perfectly illustrate how communities might orient infrastructures for closeness – as in gay men’s cruising – or for division – as in racially-segregated toilets in apartheid South Africa. Indeed, these infrastructures become an ideological battleground, as exemplified by anti-trans lobbyist obsession with gender policing in public toilets. While both uses of public toilets could not be any further from each other, they highlight that ‘there is power in the sewers’ (Wilson, 2016, p. 248). Mundane infrastructures such as public washrooms might be taken for granted but they express power when specific bodies are excluded or when they become zones of radical intimacy, reclamation, and activism.

Moving away from public washrooms back to the digital, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) mixes the technical skills of hosting computer servers with the affective labour of hosting customers. IaaS is a rising model in web-hosting wherein service providers use cloud-computing to deliver hardware such as servers and software such as virtual machines (Bhardwaj, Jain and Jain, 2010). Under this model, programmers do not have to buy server computers where they would store images and videos for their websites or apps. They would not need to deal with the endless process of installing operating systems on these servers and setting up their virtual environment with relevant prerequisites. They would instead pay for the services of a reliable provider who may host their content so they can focus on design and technical functionality of their apps or websites. A capitalist model par excellence, IaaS separates the labour from the product – the frontend from the backend; the wait staff from the chefs and porters at the back of the restaurant; and so on – in a manner that the producers of a given app may never own the infrastructure on which they have built their software. In essence, under IaaS, practitioners lose intimate knowledge of their programming environments while gaining convenience, scalability, and optimisation.

It should come as no surprise that the same large companies that dominate the technology sector are also the main IaaS providers (Statista, 2024). The usual names–Amazon, Google, and Microsoft–hold the majority of the market. In 2021, Amazon demonstrated that ‘there is power in the servers’–to paraphrase Wilson (2016, p. 248)–when it withdrew the right-wing app Parler from Amazon Web Service (AWS) for allowing violent content that went against Amazon’s terms of service (Novet, 2021). This decision occurred in response to the January 6th 2021 US Capitol attack. Amazon stated that Parler had not controlled the posts that encouraged the violent insurrection. Even as Amazon eventually stopped Parler from accessing its cloud servers, it is important to note that the app had been on AWS since 2018. Essentially, AWS infrastructure enabled the gestation of hate for three years on Parler that contributed to the January 6 attacks. Before the patriotic disdain that led to the failure of Parler’s/Amazon’s infrastructure was a capitalistic ambivalence. In both cases of failure and maintenance, there is an affect that is generated and maintained in infrastructure.

It is due to this affective power, that servers are a key concern in feminist infrastructure. One manifesto declares that a feminist server as ‘a situated technology. [… that is] run for and by a community that cares enough for her in order to make her exist’ (Snelting, 2013). One of the earliest documented feminist servers, Syster Server Syster Server is run by feminists using Free and Open Source Software. They run workshops that act as spaces where people might learn sysadmin skills. They currently maintain a feminist video platform server using PeerTube. See https://systerserver.net for more, notes that the maintenance of a server is an act of care (Wessalowski and Karagianni, 2023). They state that the traditional field of system administration (sysadmin) often distinguishes the process of setting up and maintaining a server infrastructure from care, even as the practice requires thought and consideration. As with the broader field of computing, sysadmin is masculinised and the affective power of the servers they maintain is devalued. Alternatively, feminist servers ‘set out to explore non-scalable ways of forming networks of solidarity and care among themselves and beyond. [...] They make space for ways of relating differently to each other and (with) technology’ (Wessalowski and Karagianni, 2023, pp. 203-204). Syster Server reiterate this statement on the alternative possibilities of relationality in feminist servers, in their contribution to the FSF-Toolkit, as they place their server as ‘an affective space for sharing and streaming videos away from centralized platforms’ (Karagianni et al, 2023). In reclaiming the affective power of servers, this form of feminist infrastructure opens up opportunities of intimacy and care within a network of computers and people.

Syster Server is one of many ‘networks of solidarity and care’ that form feminist servers and infrastructure. It is beyond the scope of this article to recount a full history of feminist servers. In the mode of feminist citation, however, we would like to chant out some servers as noted in earlier scholarship:
Kéfir, Vedetas, Codigo Sur, Maddix, Cl4ndestina, Systerserver, Matriar.cat, Anarchaserver, Rhizomatica, Palabra radio, Pi-node, Tetaneutral, Framasoft, any many others... (Toupin, 2020, p. 53).

In contribution to the growing history of feminist servers, we (FSF) understand the potential of servers not only for feminist infrastructure, but also for decolonial computing. Servers, for us, are not only software but also hardware — material artefacts, ancestral totems, and heirlooms that connect the intimate and sacred to everyday life. In their form as software, servers are also virtual spaces akin to traditional archival institutions that hold, share, and recreate ideas of heritage and history. In this sense, we understand servers as both physical and virtual holding places for collective memories, histories, and materials. This understanding echoes with Anarchaserver’s statement on the role of feminist servers in “regaining control and gaining autonomy in the access and management of our data and collective memories” (spideralex, 2023).

Our experiments, which we will outline later in this paper, includes both the sysadmin work of setting up a virtual environment and the physical work of tinkering with hardware. As we are concerned with both the concrete and virtual holding of archives, we hope to design everyday objects – such as vases, sculptures, boxes – that will house our server. In this sense, we also draw from the understanding that “things," to paraphrase Elisabeth Grosz (2009, p. 126), "make our world." Servers are, indeed, a form of (re)worlding – they are things through which we make our world. By world here, we borrow from Spivak's (1985) understanding of colonisation as a way of ‘worlding’ through cartography or map-making and Stuart Hall’s (Hall, 1997), concepts and classifications of culture (such as the nation, a community, or home). Hall (1997, p. 45) notes how worldmaking emanates from our ‘fantasies, desires and imagining’ as nations, communities, and families. Alternatively, part of our decolonial practice has included visualisations — imaginations — of our autonomous feminist servers. Through our diagramming and mapping (as seen in Figure 2), we speculatively re-world from the current limitations of digital imperialism by big tech. We explore how we might hold intimate objects — passports, journals, records, video games — with care. As FSF works within academic institutions with traditions of gatekeeping, optimisation, and securitisation of knowledge, feminist care is in tension with feminist/queer autonomy. In the subsequent section we expand on autonomy as orientations from optimisation and mode of dwellings.
Figure 2: Speculative FSF server diagram imagining items and network connections.

div.head: Orientations, Autonomy and Optimisation
div.p: The notion of autonomy is vital to feminist attempts to understand oppression, subjection, and agency (Mackenzie and Stoljar, 2000, p. 3).

In the shaping of sociocultural and computational alterity, equity, and imaginaries, autonomous feminist servers ‘ensure that memory of feminist groups are properly accessible, preserved, and managed’ (TransHackFeminist, 2015). They are a heritage crafted, maintained and sustained from affective and distributed infrastructures, pluralities and modalities, from which shared values, skills and experiences have been digitally anchored. Continuously navigating access, encryption, anonymity, and justice, feminist servers counter ‘androcentrism and new forms of colonialism or exploitation at the very local level’ (Zanolli et al, 2018, p. 42). They do not only reimagine in plurality, alterity, but they also reorient from optimisation through feminist autonomy.

In this section, we adapt a queer phenomenological approach to the ongoing race of technological and human optimisation. We propose ‘a different ‘slant’ to the concept of orientation’ (Ahmed, 2006, p.4) within our current socio-technical environment. To reorient away from optimisation is to open access to black boxes right ‘down to the code’, revealing what has been hidden and normalised as a default. A queer phenomenological approach to servers does not only render visible the invisible, it also makes technology transparent by ‘bringing what is ‘behind’ to the front’ (Ahmed, 2006, p. 4). To recall the Feminist Server Manifesto, feminist servers ‘[o]pens herself to expose processes, tools, sources, habits, patterns, [...][she] takes the risk of exposing her insecurity’ (Snelting, 2013). It is therefore recognising the trap of optimisation and securitisation that we ‘orient’ and highlight the importance of local autonomous feminist infrastructures in global technological systems and economy.
As Ahmed notes (2006, p. 172), queer phenomenology is a ‘disorientation device’. It is a way to become ‘oriented’, to ‘dwell’, belong, inhabit worlds, however transient they may be.
...‘not following’ involves disorientation: it makes things oblique (Ahmed, 2006, p.177).

Employing ‘queer phenomenology’ prompts us to refocus our ‘orientation’ as a means to cultivate new consciousness and modes of ‘dwelling’. To be oriented is also “to be turned toward certain objects, those that help us to find our way” (Ahmed, 2006, p. 2). Orientation also includes those who have been alongside us or have come before us in the context of our political positioning and ‘situated dwellings’ (Ahmed 2006, p. 5). To ‘dwell’ or inhabit, is “to linger, or even to delay or postpone” (Ahmed 2006, p. 20). For instance, in our experimentations with servers, we dwell or linger in feminist worlds and in hopes to postpone dystopian technological futures. Also in our writing, we align ourselves with Sara Ahmed’s feminist and queer dwellings in other scholars such as Audre Lorde, Adrienne Rich, Donna Haraway, and Patricia Hill Collins. Our dwellings also include scholars in feminist science and technology studies such as Caroline Bassett, Ruha Benjamin, Safiya Umoja Noble, Kate O’Riordan, Judy Wajcman; and the imaginaries of Gloria Anzaldúa, Octavia Butler, Alexis Pauline Gumbs, bell hooks, Monique Wittig, and those to come.

Our experimentations and orientations towards autonomous feminist servers are a process of crafting dwellings, community building and agency. It is slow, detailed, and intimate. As with other feminist servers, it is also ephemeral and precarious. As Ahmed (2006, p. 20) notes, ‘[i]f orientation is a matter of how we reside, or how we clear space that is familiar, then orientations also take time and require giving up time’. Autonomous feminist infrastructures/servers are always ‘oriented’ in the enactment of their dwellings, inhabiting a temporal misalignment with global systems. This is because optimisation is often framed by scaling up, speeding up, and the impulse of capitalist accumulation to expand, globalise and gobble up. We addressed the effect of this impulse in the context of machine learning earlier in this paper, noting how the optimisation of big data results in automated discriminations. While feminist autonomy clashes with this hegemonic system, it allows space for slowing down/up and care-ful building of affective infrastructures.

Subsequently, to maintain and care for autonomous feminist infrastructures/servers within corporate communication technology and academic institutions is to negotiate inhabitings and dwellings through displacements and intimate exposures, intentional or forced. It is to accept the precarious reality that the borders are never fixed – institutions may push for a form of (im)migration, where the archives that hold our collective memories may inhabit the uninhabitable. That noted, the very presence of autonomous feminist infrastructures in institutions means that we might disorient optimisation. This follows the feminist STS understanding that digital and computational technology can both subscribe to or disrupt normative paths. Orienting our servers towards autonomy and disorienting optimisation ultimately connects back to our feminist affective practices that allows for “intimacy of bodies and their dwelling places” (Ahmed, 2006, p. 8). In the two-way transformations of our infrastructures and our socio-technical environment, care gets reoriented as a form of affective power and highlights the (im)possibility of autonomy. In the next section, we discuss our attempts to build an autonomous feminist server together. We negotiate the aforementioned tensions in embedding feminist affective infrastructures within globalised institutional technological systems. Seeking autonomy against technodeterministic optimisation, we highlight the (im)possibilities of building infrastructure together.

div.head: Building Together: A Discussion on Our Experiments
div.p: Figure 3: An image showing the Raspberry Pi cluster connected to a router via an Ethernet Network splitter. The router (middle) is connected to an ethernet wall port and connected to the splitter (on the left). Each individual Raspberry Pi is connected to a port on the splitter. The connection moves in the direction: Ethernet to Router to Splitter to Raspberry Pi.

...What would be the purposes and principles of a feminist server? Can feminist servers support women, feminists and GLBTQI in their fight for having their rights such as freedom of expression and opinion respected? Can we create trust among us to develop cooperative approaches to the management of those spaces of resistance and transformation? (Toupin and Hache, 2015, p. 24)

The speculative FSF server diagram (Figure 2) encapsulates our hopes and imaginations for our server experiment. In many respects, our attempts to build an autonomous server were based on an ambition to return to an intimate knowledge of the infrastructures we so heavily rely upon. We wanted to understand the code, the machine, the processes, the points of failure, and the challenges of returning to a decentralised framework of digital technology. Recognising the history of networked technologies such as Bulletin Board Systems (BBS) which supported much feminist, and queer, community development and knowledge sharing, and which required specific knowledge to host and sustain an online community (McKinney, 2020; Dame-Griff, 2023), we wanted to experiment and test the limits of our understanding – we wanted to identify the limits of autonomy within institutional infrastructures. While regarded as precarious infrastructures, in the main, bulletin board systems relied upon a network of individuals who had an inherent, value based, interest in both upholding the network, and of being connected to the individuals or the community it created and sustained. BBS users and domain owners were orientated to the technology for reasons other than commercial gain, as they sought out like-minded members/individuals with shared values and interests. BBS, the precursor to our current social media platforms, were decentered from large tech companies, and instead relied on individuals having the technical knowledge to run the network. We wanted to return to this form of decentralisation, and explore this return to autonomy as a form of feminist critical practice. practised by many social movements’ (Toupin et al, 2015) provides ‘different governance models’, from which autonomy is ‘a desire for freedom, self-valorisation and mutual aid’ (Toupin et al, 2015). Critically, however, they are never quite complete as this work is embedded in and co-dependent on larger corporate communication systems, networks, and technologies (Chevalier et al, 2023; Wessalowski and Karagianni, 2023).

Our experiment took place over the course of 9 months (2022-23). We, that is the authors, Ranju Upadhyay (FSF Programmer) and Alex Peverett (FSF Technician), started with a small-scale ambition – to host the project’s archive (Omeka). Additionally, we sought autonomy through a solution that was repairable, scalable, and sustainable, as well as accessible (financially and technically). We investigated various options, including using old PCs from our universities’, but decided to build a Raspberry Pi cluster (seen in Figure 3) since it supported a more accessible approach repair and would be portable to be housed in everyday objects. https://www.raspberrypi.com/tutorials/cluster-raspberry-pi-tutorial/ Our ambition was to build together, as a collective, one cluster at Maynooth University (Ireland), and one at the University of Sussex. We prioritised process, understanding, and documentation over an efficient and optimised output. We kept detailed notes on various aspects of the build which, in most tutorials, were never documented or were brushed over as minor details. At every step we questioned the pursuit of autonomy given various infrastructural and technical limitations, embracing that ‘the notion of autonomy is vital to feminist attempts to understand oppression, subjection, and agency’ (Mackenzie and Stoljar, 2000, p. 3). For example, can we be truly autonomous when we are reliant on:

list.item: the electrical grid - could we be solar powered?
in our case, university access to the internet. Which brings about its own set of problems that clash with our motivations, as stated in the previous section.
a global supply chain, which at the time of our experiment meant we could only buy three Raspberry Pi’s, thus limiting our capacity.

div.p: These issues are not trivial, they highlight the infrastructural entanglements in which we exist, and which limit our options and ability to be fully autonomous. In addition, as Ranju Upadhyay states in their 2023 panel contribution in Algorithms for Her 2 (2023) conference,

While open-source software (at OS level and application level) has made the software side of things more accessible and independent, the technical infrastructure it inhabits remains largely proprietary. This creates a challenge when developing any technical DH tool that is fully autonomous and seeks to engage with feminist principles (Chevalier et al, 2023)
In the same panel, Upadhyay compared using their university’s subscription to Microsoft (MS) Azure Cloud and building a Pi cluster. They asked, ‘what is wrong with having it in a commercial cloud?’

This is a very hierarchical structure with the greatest control lying with the MS. We must accept several terms and conditions set by MS before we get to our server (i.e. virtual machine)... Our knowledge and understanding is also clouded! e.g. we must move hardware when MS tells us to, we must upgrade when MS says it has stopped supporting a component, our access condition is decided by MS i.e. one must be a staff member of the university to gain server access (which is problematic in collaborative project like ours)... It adds abstraction and we lose Intimacy... It is corporate empowerment as opposed to community empowerment.

Why use it then? It is quick, it is relatively easy, it is available in abundance, it is available 24/7 and as long as we agree with the T&Cs and keep paying the bills, it can do most of the things for us! We can offload maintenance responsibility back to MS. [...]
In [our experimental] set up we understand every layer of [our server]. It removes the layers of abstraction. It restores intimacy (Chevalier et al, 2023).

The restoration of intimacy is extended not only by knowledge but by our embodied experiences. Unlike a cloud server, we were able to tinker with our Pi Cluster. We are able to touch and adjust all the screws on the nodes in the cluster (see Figure 4). We are able to see which server is down by monitoring the lights on the boards. Most importantly, we are able to build affect around the object — the thing in itself — through the ways we as a community (including our non-human companions) interact with the Pi Cluster.
Figure 4: A three-panel image showing the Raspberry Pi clusters. Panels 1 and 2 show the hardware setup and finalisation in Sussex. Panel 3 shows the final setup in Maynooth.

In this respect, restoring intimacy to infrastructure through technological and embodied knowing, is a form of reorientation. Our autonomy from the institutional Microsoft subscription orients us towards (im)possibilities for alternative pathways, places and spaces from which autonomous feminist legacies can be imagined, inhabited and maintained. As we carefully placed screws onto the plates that held each machine on the cluster, we embodied an ethics of care that is involved both in the development of feminist infrastructure, its maintenance, and ultimately care for the content it will one day host. When we rethink our (re)orientations towards affective infrastructures, they become entwined with human, digital rights, and security. As Foz (2022, p. 11) states, ‘digital care’ is intimate since ‘the online and offline are indissociable’, meaning ‘what affects our data also impacts our bodies’. Governance in these spaces, is therefore, governance of our bodies, thus, ‘in the digital care perspective, taking care of our data is also taking care of our body and this care should be done every day, as a habit, a culture, politics’ (Foz, 2022, p. 11).

As we worked on the cluster, we slowly realised how much of a project it would be to host the project’s archive via Omeka on our server. Our collective building process was slow. As mentioned earlier, the tutorials and technical documents we used as guidance were often dated and assumed a prior knowledge that frequently sent us into tangential routes in search of fixes. In addition, mundane situations in computing such as cross-compatibility across different operating systems, download times or writing operating systems on to storage cards, took much of our time in our collective workshops. This meant that we were only able to physically assemble the cluster, set-up the concurrent configurations in our Sussex and Maynooth experiments, and finally, run some test scripts in Python. Stopping at the configuration of our server infrastructure was also an act of care for us. As some members of Syster Server write,

[p]ractices of care and maintenance within feminist servers must be understood as negotiations of collective responsibility. [...Sysadmins on feminist servers] participate according to their availabilities and thereby extend the principle of care towards themselves by taking into account the different intersectional precarities that deﬁne their situation (Wessalowski and Karagianni, 2023, p.197).

Having different capacities (including time), we collectively decided that the server configuration was a sufficient point to stop for future speculations and real world applications. With that noted, we still built the cluster together – and that is a success in itself. As stated earlier, we did not prioritise an efficient, optimised final product. Instead, due to our relative autonomy, we oriented ourselves towards the slow process of building together, with shared ethos of autonomy, collective care, and guided by our troubled histories and various dwellings. Currently, the server is not active. However, we hope to extend its use for future projects and imaginaries. In this sense, the heritage of the server itself will be passed on and our configured infrastructure will be repurposed towards other feminist intimacies (Wilson, 2016, p.262).

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Throughout this paper, we have situated autonomous feminist infrastructures within the technological terrain. From the retelling or revealing troubled histories that have excluded women from computing, to expanding on the context of our wider research project, to applying feminist theory to understanding infrastructures and autonomy, to expanding on our own collective experiments, we have examined modes of feminist infrastructure-making within (im)possible constraints. Although our experiments are not finished, they demonstrate our move towards (im)possible autonomy and our aim to resist the dominant socio-technical, intervening on the aforementioned historical bias. As we have noted earlier, our work exists within a space — a dwelling — of theorists and practitioners that have shaped our feminist imaginaries. Our project of an autonomous feminist server configuration is still ongoing as our cluster, our thinking, and affective imaginaries will continue to be developed and repurposed.

We have explored affect in infrastructure-making, focusing on autonomous feminist servers, noting opportunities to build with care. Our autonomous feminist servers are one that resonates with Wilson’s (2016) thinking on intimacy, infrastructure and power, where the local community have access to “relocate their conditions of possibility and relations and forces of production” (Stoler, 2006, p. 13). Feminist autonomous infrastructures/servers - although hopeful - are never a destination, an arrival, but a process of collective power/care from which recognition, shared ethos for change, for justice are always shifting and transforming. We close this paper, with an adaptation of our developing manifesto on autonomy — noting that autonomy, as our work, is an orientation for us and not a final destination:
autonomy is care.

Machines get fuelled, serviced, maintained, repaired in people automation. Yet nurturing only service passivity. Care - although often framed as feminine labour, when situated from autonomous feminist infrastructures ethics of care reframes power. As care becomes entangled with encryption, cybersecurity, legacy, capacity building.
autonomy is crafting-hacking.

When pathways are not paved, there is a need to dig your own. When tools to make new pathways only exist from rigid infrastructures and impossible heritage, there is a need to build your own. It is from the collective power/care in Do-It-Together, in hacking, processing, maintaining that crafting objects and worlds from which inhabiting and collective memory, legacies are shaped.
autonomy is intimacy.
When autonomy is not given but crafted, shared from the borders.
autonomy is slow.

Slow is strategic. It is stepping back from techno intimacy, to gain oversight and orientation in the impact of moving faster, as our vision is shortened, as our vision is already focus on what comes at us – setting-up a ripple of automated ‘affect’ and high capacity process (Chevalier et al, 2023).
